Greater flamingo chicks emerge from eggs incubated for approximately 28.5 days [ab = approximately 28.5 days] at a temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C], a thermal regime that reflects the consistent brooding behavior typical of this species. Upon hatching, neonates are covered in white down and weigh approximately 76 grams [Wwb = approximately 76 grams], a mass that is relatively substantial for a precocial chick and provides sufficient endogenous reserves for the first few days of life. This initial body mass is critical for the chick's ability to thermoregulate and to begin following its parents within the shallow alkaline lakes and coastal lagoons that constitute its foraging habitat. The precise control of incubation temperature, as documented by Bech and Johansen in their 1979 study, ensures that development proceeds at an optimal rate. Maintaining a steady nest temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C] is energetically demanding for the adult, as it requires constant shuffling and adjustment of the single egg held on the webbed feet. The incubation period itself is remarkably consistent across colonies, with only minor variation attributable to local ambient conditions, and it represents a foundational milestone in the life cycle of this iconic wading bird.

Once hatched, the chick undergoes a rapid period of somatic growth, transitioning from its initial neonatal mass to the far larger dimensions of a fully-grown adult. The ultimate wet weight attained by a mature Greater flamingo is around 3000 grams [Wwi = around 3000 grams], although adults can range between 2 and 4 kilograms depending on sex, nutritional status, and geographic location. Achieving this adult body mass requires an extended period of parental provisioning with crop milk, a lipid- and protein-rich secretion produced in the upper digestive tract. This high-energy diet fuels the chick's development through its fledging stage, which occurs at 36 days after hatching [tx = 36 days after hatching] at a temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]. At 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], the typical core body temperature of active adult birds, the fledgling is capable of sustained flight and begins to forage independently in the shallow waters of its natal lagoon. This milestone marks a critical transition from complete dependence on parental care to a semi-independent juvenile existence, though young birds often remain in crèches for several additional weeks.

Following fledging, the young flamingo enters a protracted juvenile phase characterized by gradual plumage maturation and continued growth. The attainment of puberty occurs at 108 days after hatching [tp = 108 days after hatching], measured at the species' active metabolic temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]. At this point, gonadal development is sufficiently advanced to allow eventual reproductive function, though actual breeding is typically deferred for several more years. This delay is common among long-lived colonial waterbirds, where the acquisition of a suitable nesting territory and the development of pair bonds require considerable time and social experience. The juvenile period is also marked by a gradual change in feather coloration, as the greyish down and early juvenal plumage give way to the pale pink hues that intensify with age and dietary intake of carotenoid pigments from brine shrimp and algae. During this time, the birds form large flocks and engage in complex synchronized group displays that reinforce social cohesion.

This first breeding event is a significant investment, requiring the establishment of a mud-nest mound on a suitable salt flat or island that is safe from terrestrial predators and tidal inundation. The delay between reaching sexual maturity and initiating reproduction is thought to be mediated by the need to accumulate sufficient body condition and to learn the intricacies of courtship rituals. Experienced breeders enjoy higher fledging success than first-time parents, highlighting the role of learning and social coordination.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Greater flamingo is approximately 44 years [am = approximately 44 years], measured at 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], making it one of the longer-lived species within the family Phoenicopteridae. This extended longevity, coupled with a low annual reproductive rate of approximately one brood per year [F_R_i = approximately one brood per year] with a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], places the species firmly within a slow life-history strategy characteristic of large, colonial, semiprecocial birds. Such a strategy relies heavily on high adult survival to offset low fecundity, and any environmental perturbation that increases adult mortality, such as habitat degradation or extreme climatic events, can have profound population-level consequences. The species also shows remarkable physiological resilience, tolerating high salinity and temperature extremes in its preferred alkaline lake habitats. Captive individuals have been documented to survive well past the half-century mark, underscoring the species' inherent robustness. Comparative analyses with other long-lived waterbirds suggest that this longevity is intimately linked to a low metabolic rate and effective antioxidant defenses.
